newsitem.title: UK: Channel Tunnel built to withstand fire,earthquake.
newsitem.headline: Channel Tunnel built to withstand fire,earthquake.

text.p: The fire in the Channel Tunnel between France and Britain on Tuesday was the first serious incident in the undersea link and put to the test systems designed to guard against disasters ranging from guerrilla attacks to earthquakes.
Tunnel operators Eurotunnel have always insisted that it is "at least twenty times safer travelling through the tunnel than when travelling by conventional railways".
During the meticulous planning of the 51-km (32-mile) tunnel, opened two years ago, each step was scrutinised by an Anglo-French intergovernmental commission.
Security systems were designed to guard against worst case scenarios including fire, guerrilla attacks and even rabid dogs crossing from France into Britain.
The tunnel was also built to withstand the worst earthquake to have hit the south coast of England in the last millennium.
A central service shaft runs between the two main rail tunnels, allowing firefighters and other rescue services access to trains with entrances every 50 metres.

The service tunnel is also the main evacuation point for passengers, allowing them to be treated for injuries there before being led to safety either by walking or boarding a train in the adjoining rail tunnel.
Shuttle trains are fireproof and have fire detection systems and a range of firefighting equipment on board.
Closed circuit television cameras monitor the interior of all shuttle wagons throughout the journey and there is a halon gas fire suppression system which is safe for people being evacuated.
Firefighters on the French and British sides of the tunnel hold regular training exercises and use a freshwater main running the length of the tunnel to douse fires.
Eurotunnel bosses said safety procedures overnight had gone to plan.
"We have a bi-national emergency plan which we had followed exactly and worked exactly as we anticipated," said Clive Durrant, director of safety for Eurotunnel.
"The operation was led by the French although 100 fire officers from Kent have been involved in containing the incident," he told reporters.
